title: Cold open — does Claude already know how to make a good chart?
text: Someone assumed Claude already knows how to make a good chart. Not quite. It gets told what to check in a kit it reads before drawing. Here's what that kit actually spells out. The kit has five

title: Anatomy — chartkit primitives + data helpers
text: Primitives and three data helpers. Theme sets matplotlib RC params and returns resolved colors. The key field is that foreground colors derive from background luminance. Pass a dark background and you get a correct dark chart automatically. Pallet builds in colors from a base hex, cycles a list, or falls back to the series defaults. Finish adds the typographic frame, left aligned bold title, muted and provenance caption. Save writes PNG, SVG, or both and returns paths. Write HTML produces a self-contained interactive page by inlining React, React DOM, React as in Recharts from a local third-party directory. The file opens offline with no CDN independency. The three data helpers address specific gotchas. Zero fill days fills calendar gaps in a time series, but skip it when zeros would be a lie because the data is sparsely sampled, not absent. Rolling mean is trailing and early points average whatever exists so far. Do not center it. Log floor gives a lower bound for bar charts on log scales where value equals the axis minimum. All three are optional. Use them only when they fit. The absolute path to graphing scripts directory must go into sys.path, not a relative path, because the working directory is the user's project. title: Design — four-step workflow + judgement defaults
text: Four steps are look at the data and decide what it deserves, infer colors from context, Tailwind config, CSS variables, brand guidelines, and semantic meaning, write the script, and render and look at the result before handing it over. The render and look step is explicit. Check labels for legibility, nothing overlapping, colors distinguishable, the story of the data visible. Fix and re-render until it is right. The judgment section gives defaults with explicit permission to deviate when the data argues for it. Five defaults worth knowing. Rotate X labels only when they would otherwise collide. Short labels stay horizontal. Cap bar width when there are a few categories. Label bars with their values when there are roughly a dozen or fewer. Rank categorical bars by value unless the categories have a natural order. A title states what the chart shows, not the chart type. Not the column name. Legends only when there is more than one series. Annotate the chart with what matters. A deploy line, a threshold, the peak, the anomaly. An annotation the reader did not need is clutter.

title: Both directions — documented plainly vs. easy to miss
text: So, does having this kit mean Claude always makes the right chart? Not exactly. Where the kit spells something out plainly, the first step judgment call, colors that adapt to the background, an offline file that just works, Claude follows it and skips the mistake entirely. Where it's a placeholder string swapped by hand or one phrase covering an edge case, Claude can still get it wrong the same way a person skimming the same page would. A charting kit doesn't give

title: Carry-out
text: Claude good taste. It gives Claude judgment defaults to start from and a few sharp edges marked and Claude only dodges the edges the kit actually marks.

title: Your turn
text: Your turn. Here's the prompt. Read it with me. Give Claude a data set you've never charted before, something with a real gap in it or no obvious color to reach for. Before it writes any chart code, ask what it's going to check in the data first and where the colors are coming from. Then have it render the result, look at the PNG itself and say what it would fix before handing it to you. Claude graphing. Lay 'em in for bear.
